heroCta.title: Start with the IND naturalisation page
heroCta.supportingText: This guide orients Highly Skilled Migrants and other expats to Dutch nationality. Confirm eligibility, renunciation rules, fees, and documents on IND and government.nl — we do not replace official assessment.

quickAnswers.label: Two main adult routes
quickAnswers.value: Naturalisation (most common after ~5 years lawful stay) or option (narrower legal categories; often faster, usually no integration proof or renunciation).

quickAnswers.label: Dual nationality
quickAnswers.value: Naturalisation usually requires renouncing your other nationality unless an IND / Dutch-law exception applies. Check your home country’s rules too.

quickAnswers.label: Inburgering
quickAnswers.value: Naturalisation usually needs civic integration proof at least at A2 (or an exemption). Option usually does not require demonstrating integration.

quickAnswers.label: Not permanent residence
quickAnswers.value: PR is a stay status. Citizenship changes nationality — passport, voting, and EU citizenship follow after you complete the ceremony.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Dutch citizenship is the step beyond long-term residence. It can bring a Dutch passport, voting rights in national elections, and EU citizenship — but it is a separate legal process from permanent residence, with fees, documents, and often renunciation of another nationality.

This page is the authoritative ExpatLife guide for that planning: naturalisation versus option, dual nationality caveats, what inburgering actually unlocks (and when it does not), and how to sequence your gemeente and the IND. It is not legal advice and does not restate decision rules as if ExpatLife were the IND. Complex cases (mixed permit history, children, prior refusals, abroad applications) usually need qualified nationality advice.

callout.title: Orientation only — confirm on IND and government.nl
callout.text: Fees, exceptions, and renunciation rules change. Use IND naturalisation and option pages plus government.nl dual citizenship guidance as the source of truth for your situation.

sections.heading: Naturalisation vs option
body: Foreign nationals usually become Dutch through naturalisation or through the option procedure (optie). They are not interchangeable. Government.nl and IND describe option as a shorter procedure available only to people who belong to specific groups defined by law. Naturalisation is the route most adult Highly Skilled Migrants and other long-term residents use after qualifying lawful residence.

IND notes several advantages of option when you qualify: you usually do not have to renounce your other nationality, you do not have to demonstrate that you are sufficiently integrated, and costs are lower than naturalisation. Do not assume you qualify for option just because you have lived in the Netherlands for many years.

Often faster; usually no integration demonstration; usually no renunciation — confirm on IND option page.

Not an application path for most adult expats — see government.nl becoming a Dutch citizen.

callout.title: Check option before you assume naturalisation
callout.text: If any IND option category might apply, read the option page first. Applying for the wrong route wastes fees and months.

sections.heading: Dual nationality caveats
body: The Netherlands generally wants to limit dual citizenship. Government.nl states that people who acquire Dutch nationality through naturalisation are, as a rule, required to give up their other citizenship if possible (the renunciation requirement).

Exceptions exist — for example when your origin country does not allow renunciation, when you automatically lose the other nationality on becoming Dutch, or other situations government.nl and IND list (including certain refugee and marriage-related cases). Exceptions are case-specific; forum lists are a common source of mistakes.

Your origin country’s law still matters. Some countries never allow renunciation; others treat naturalisation abroad as automatic loss of citizenship whether or not the Netherlands required renunciation. Check both Dutch and home-country rules before you apply — and before you attend the ceremony.

rows: You undertake to renounce the other nationality after becoming Dutch; failure to try can risk revocation.
IND renouncing your nationality + government.nl dual citizenship
You may keep the other nationality when Dutch law allows — document the ground on the application.
Usually no renunciation — still confirm for your option category.
Military service, inheritance, or automatic loss rules can still apply even if the Netherlands allows dual status.

callout.title: Policy-sensitive and personal
callout.text: Dual nationality rules are politically sensitive and change. Read current government.nl dual citizenship guidance and IND renunciation pages rather than outdated blog posts.

sections.heading: What inburgering actually unlocks (and what it does not)
body: For naturalisation, IND states you must fulfil the integration requirement: normally a civic integration exam at at least language level A2, unless you are exempted. That is the citizenship-facing proof — often a diploma from DUO exams, a recognised exemption, or other evidence IND lists on civic integration for naturalisation.

Passing inburgering does not by itself make you Dutch, grant permanent residence, or skip renunciation. It unlocks one of the conditions for naturalisation (and often for permanent residence earlier). Option applicants usually do not have to demonstrate integration — that is one reason option is attractive when you qualify.

Highly Skilled Migrants are often not under inburgeringsplicht on a temporary work permit, yet still need integration proof later for naturalisation. Start exams early enough that certificates exist before you book a gemeente appointment — see our inburgering guide for Wi 2021 / B1 context versus the A2 naturalisation floor.

rows: Usually yes as a prerequisite (A2 diploma or IND-recognised exemption).
Often yes for the secure-residence integration requirement — separate from nationality.
PR guide + IND secure residence page
No — HSM stays tied to recognised-sponsor rules.

callout.title: DUO runs exams; IND assesses the requirement
callout.text: Book and complete civic integration exams via DUO / inburgeren.nl. IND decides whether your diploma or exemption meets naturalisation conditions.

sections.heading: Typical naturalisation requirements (high-level orientation)
body: IND’s naturalisation page is the checklist source of truth. At a high level, adult applicants usually need to be 18+, prove identity and nationality, show consecutive lawful residence (often five years, with published exceptions), hold an eligible residence right through the ceremony date, meet integration, clear public-order rules, renounce other nationality unless excepted, and be willing to make the declaration of solidarity at the ceremony.

Citizenship and permanent residence share a planning horizon for many expats, but they are separate steps. You can hold permanent residence for years before naturalising — or naturalise when eligible if your residence purpose and documents already fit. Permit gaps, absences, and late renewals affect both paths.

rows: Often 5 consecutive years with a valid permit; shorter paths exist in listed exceptions.
IND exceptions to the 5-year term for naturalisation
Permanent, long-term EU resident, temporary with non-temporary purpose, or other IND-listed rights.
Civic integration exam at least at A2, or exemption / other accepted proof.
You must not be a danger to public order or national security.

callout.title: Fees and decision period
callout.text: IND publishes fees and states a decision period (commonly described as up to 12 months for naturalisation). Confirm current amounts and timelines on IND — do not rely on copied figures from older articles.

sections.heading: How to sequence the application (orientation)
body: Follow IND’s process rather than inventing a parallel checklist. Applications for naturalisation are submitted at your municipality; the gemeente does a first check and forwards the file to the IND. You become Dutch only after a positive decision, the Royal Decree, and attendance at the naturalisation ceremony (within the deadline IND states — typically within one year of the positive decision).
After the ceremony you can apply for a Dutch passport or identity card at the gemeente, then complete any required renunciation steps with your other country’s authorities.
steps: Confirm whether option or naturalisation fits — read both IND pages before booking an appointment.
Collect identity, birth, residence, and integration (or exemption) documents IND lists; legalise foreign documents where required.
Book a gemeente appointment; pay the fee; include minor children only when IND child rules are met.
Track the IND decision (My IND where available); keep renewing your residence right if it would expire mid-procedure.
If positive: attend the naturalisation ceremony, make the declaration of solidarity, then apply for a Dutch passport and complete renunciation if required.

callout.title: Ceremony is mandatory
callout.text: A positive IND decision alone does not make you Dutch. You must attend the naturalisation ceremony within the stated period or you will not receive Dutch nationality.

faq.q: What is the difference between naturalisation and option?
faq.a: Naturalisation is the common adult route after qualifying lawful residence and integration proof, usually with a renunciation requirement. Option is a faster procedure for specific legal categories; IND notes you usually do not renounce or demonstrate integration. Check the IND option page before assuming naturalisation is your only path.

faq.q: Do I have to give up my current passport?
faq.a: For naturalisation, the Netherlands generally requires renunciation of your other nationality unless an exception applies. Option usually does not require renunciation. Always verify Dutch and home-country rules — some countries forbid renunciation or automatically strip citizenship when you naturalise elsewhere.

faq.q: Does passing inburgering make me Dutch?
faq.a: No. Inburgering (or an IND-recognised exemption) usually unlocks the integration condition for naturalisation and often for permanent residence. You still need residence, public-order, and other IND conditions — and you only become Dutch after the ceremony.

faq.q: Is Dutch citizenship the same as permanent residence?
faq.a: No. Permanent residence is a long-term stay permit. Citizenship changes your nationality. Many people hold permanent residence for years before deciding on naturalisation.

faq.q: How long before I can apply?
faq.a: Many naturalisation routes look at five consecutive years of lawful residence, but IND publishes exceptions for shorter periods. Permit gaps and absences matter. Confirm on the IND naturalisation and exceptions pages — not on calculators alone.

Naturalisation and option applications are submitted at your municipality (gemeente). The IND assesses naturalisation after the gemeente forwards the file. Option decisions follow the municipality / King process described on the IND option page.

faq.q: Does my child automatically become Dutch if I naturalise?
faq.a: Children may be included under specific age, residence, and consent rules — not automatically. Read IND requirements for minor children and post-naturalisation rather than assuming inclusion.

faq.q: What if I plan to leave the Netherlands after naturalising?
faq.a: Citizenship does not remove tax, pension, or dual-nationality questions when you emigrate. If departure is possible, read our leaving tax guide alongside nationality planning.
